sections.title: Basic Concept of Data Sufficiency
sections.content: In Data Sufficiency, the question does not ask for the final value. Instead, it asks whether the given statements are sufficient to find the answer. You do not need to fully solve the problem; you only need to determine if the information is enough. Usually, two statements (I) and (II) are provided.

sections.title: Standard Answer Pattern
sections.content: The common answer options are: (1) Statement I alone is sufficient. (2) Statement II alone is sufficient. (3) Both statements together are sufficient. (4) Neither statement is sufficient. While solving, check each statement individually first, then evaluate them together.

sections.title: Age-Based Questions (Past/Future Ratios)
sections.content: If the present age is x and the ratio from 5 years ago is given, use (x − 5). If the ratio after 5 years is given, use (x + 5). In Data Sufficiency, check whether a single equation gives a unique value or if there are two variables. If there are two unknowns and only one equation, the information is not sufficient.

sections.title: Profit & Loss / Simple Interest
sections.content: Profit = SP − CP. Profit% = (Profit / CP) × 100. Simple Interest = (P × R × T) / 100. If the question provides only percentages but not the principal or cost price, check whether the percentage alone can determine the answer. Often, one statement gives the relationship between CP and SP but not their exact values.

sections.title: Average-Based Questions
sections.content: Average = Total Sum / Number of Items. If the number of students and the average are given, the total marks can be calculated. If only the average is given but the number is missing, the information is incomplete. The same rule applies to team scores in cricket.

sections.title: Time and Work (A and B Working Together)
sections.content: If A completes a work in x days, then A's one-day work = 1/x. If A and B work together, their combined work rates are added. In Data Sufficiency, check whether a statement gives the total work rate or only individual rates.

sections.title: 2–3 Step Evaluation Strategy
sections.content: Step 1: Carefully read the question. Step 2: Evaluate Statement I alone. Step 3: Evaluate Statement II alone. Step 4: Evaluate both statements together. If at any step you get one unique answer, that statement(s) is sufficient.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Trying to fully solve the problem. 2. Combining both statements immediately. 3. Assuming that a ratio will always give a definite value. 4. Ignoring the number of items in average problems.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: The goal in Data Sufficiency is to determine 'Can the answer be found?' rather than 'What is the answer?' Always check each statement separately. If a statement leads to one unique value, it is sufficient; otherwise, it is not.

tricks.title: Check Statement I First
tricks.explanation: Always evaluate Statement I independently first. If it gives a unique answer, there is no need to proceed further.
tricks.example: If Statement I alone gives one definite present age, it is sufficient.

tricks.title: Two Unknowns = Insufficient Data
tricks.explanation: If there are two variables but only one equation, the answer cannot be determined.
tricks.example: A ratio is given but the actual difference is not provided — insufficient information.

tricks.title: Number is Necessary in Average
tricks.explanation: The total cannot be calculated from the average alone unless the number of items is known.
tricks.example: Average is 50 but the number of students is not given — insufficient.

tricks.title: Profit% Does Not Always Give Amount
tricks.explanation: Percentage alone does not determine the exact CP or SP.
tricks.example: Profit is 20% but CP is not given — insufficient.

tricks.title: Think in Work Rate (Time & Work)
tricks.explanation: Instead of days, think in terms of one-day work.
tricks.example: If A completes work in 5 days, then A's one-day work is 1/5.

tricks.title: Combine Both Statements
tricks.explanation: If Statements I and II are individually insufficient but together give a unique answer, then they are sufficient.
tricks.example: Statement I gives ratio, Statement II gives difference — together they determine the age.

tricks.title: More Than One Answer = Insufficient
tricks.explanation: If a statement allows multiple possible answers, it is not sufficient.
tricks.example: Age could be 20 or 25 — statement is insufficient.

tricks.title: Avoid Full Calculation
tricks.explanation: In Data Sufficiency, full calculation is not necessary. Just check whether a unique answer is possible.
tricks.example: If a solvable equation forms, it may already be sufficient.

tricks.title: Ratio Means Multiples
tricks.explanation: If the ratio is 2:3, the actual values are 2x and 3x. The value of x must be known.
tricks.example: If x cannot be determined, the information is insufficient.

tricks.title: Look for a Unique Answer
tricks.explanation: If a statement leads to only one definite value, it is sufficient.
tricks.example: Simple Interest gives one unique principal value — sufficient.
